Nscale lost $1.7bn before filing to list.

The London-founded AI data centre group wants a $35bn New York float. It has raised $13bn in two years and signed over $100bn in contracts.

Yet it burned through cash at a rate that dwarfs its $308m revenue in the first nine months of the year. The company now admits it needs fresh capital within twelve months just to fulfil deals already signed.

The hiring freeze covers office roles only. Headcount has still more than tripled this year, from 300 to over 1,100.

Sheryl Sandberg joined the board in February and stands to receive up to $90m in shares if the float succeeds. Several senior hires have followed from her Meta network, and some early staff have reportedly pushed back on the company's gravitational pull toward the US.

CoreWeave shares have halved since Nscale filed, which is an uncomfortable backdrop for founder Josh Payne.

One missing sentence is keeping you trapped in routine approvals.

Every approval request lands in your inbox because nobody ever wrote down when the previous answer was "yes"

There are 9 types of approvals I keep seeing in businesses and all it takes to hand them off is a single sentence for each.

Write one line for each of the 9, then test it on the next real request that comes in

1. Discounts: approve it if the client pays on time and the discount matches one you've given before, escalate anything new

2. Refunds: approve it when the work clearly missed what the client signed, escalate when the client is disputing what was agreed

3. Supplier choices: approve it when the supplier is already on the approved list, escalate when it's a first order with someone new

4. Scope changes: approve it when the extra work fits inside the current deadline, escalate when it moves the delivery date

5. Overtime: approve it when a client deadline would otherwise be missed, escalate when it's the third week in a row

6. Software renewals: approve it when the tool was used every week last quarter, escalate when nobody can name who uses it

7. Deadline extensions: approve it when the client asks before the original date, escalate when the delay has already happened

8. Hiring a freelancer: approve it for a role you've filled the same way before, escalate for any new type of work

9. Payment terms: approve it when the client asks for the terms in your standard contract, escalate any request to change them

Each rule gets tested the first time someone uses it, and the gaps show up in the requests that still reach you

I work through this with owners because every rule written is one less message waiting for you on a Friday

Pick the decision that reached you most often and write its line today

The gap between a 12 LPA and a 40 LPA SDET is not more tools. It's this JD

Most SDETs read a Senior job post as a longer list of tools.
It isn't. It's a different job.

I took a real one. Veeam. Senior SDET, Bangalore, 8+ years.
Then I mapped every line to what the job actually tests.

Here is what each line means, and where most "senior" candidates go quiet.

1) "Design, build and scale automation frameworks"
↳ Can 300 tests still run clean after 6 months.
Most people have only written tests inside a framework someone else built. They never made the design calls themselves.

2) "Write clean, high quality automation code"
↳ Is your test code reviewed like product code.
Hardcoded data, copy-pasted locators, raw waits. That is tutorial code, not senior code.

3) "Build internal tools, mock services and data utilities"
↳ Can you unblock testing when the API isn't ready yet.
A lot of SDETs only consume test data. They have never built a mock or a data factory.

4) "Integrate suites into CI (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, GitLab)"
↳ Do your tests run headless, in parallel, and pass the same way every time.
"Works on my machine" is where most frameworks quietly die.

5) "Test plans across functional, integration, regression, performance"
↳ Can you decide what NOT to automate.
A senior knows what to skip. Automating everything usually means there is no risk model.

6) "Partner with PMs and engineers in the design phase"
↳ Can you catch the bug in the design review, before the code exists.
Most testers enter after the build is done and test what already shipped.

7) "Test REST and GraphQL APIs"
↳ Contract level checks, not status code checks.
The dangerous API bug isn't a 500. It's a 200 with the wrong body.

Read it again.
Every gap is the same gap.
You can write tests. You have never designed the system that runs them.
That is the line between an SDET and a Senior SDET.

That was my main takeaway from last week’s AI for Boards masterclass.

Boards now ask about value. In Protiviti’s 2026 survey, 63% of boards in high-AI-ROI organisations discuss AI at every meeting, against 13% in the low-ROI group. Correlation, not proof. Still a signal.

A recent Stanford study of 20 directors in regulated sectors: 70% said their board lacked clearly defined AI governance responsibility.

From inside programmes, the pitfalls look familiar:
🥔 The hot potato: nobody wants AI risk, so it lands with IT by default.
🎭 An AI committee that cannot stop a use case. Decoration.
🔄 The same team builds, controls and reports.
🪑 HR and procurement missing from the table, while they own hiring and vendor contracts.

IT should manage AI. The board must govern it. Ownership has to run across functions. A property of the system, not a box on the org chart.

One observation in the recent discussion about Indian IT brands stood out to me.
Research and development shouldn't become a priority only when a company's existing business starts facing pressure.
That sounds simple, but it can be difficult for established service companies.
When a business has reliable customers and a profitable operating model, there are strong incentives to keep improving what already works.
Hiring more people, expanding delivery centers and winning larger contracts can appear more predictable than investing in uncertain research.
The problem is that technological change rarely waits for a convenient moment.
By the time a new technology starts affecting revenue, competitors may already have years of experience developing products around it.
AI is creating exactly this kind of challenge.
Companies that mainly adopted existing software tools may find themselves competing against businesses that have invested deeply in automation, data platforms and proprietary technology.
Those investments take time to mature.
Researchers need opportunities to experiment.
Early products may not generate meaningful revenue.
Some projects will fail.
A company focused entirely on short-term financial performance may struggle to justify that uncertainty.
But avoiding it can create a larger problem later.
I think established IT firms need a more deliberate balance between serving existing customers and building capabilities for future markets.
The strongest research programs don't necessarily produce immediate headlines.
Their value often becomes visible when the rest of the industry suddenly needs something the company has been developing for years.

Imagine hiring an IT services company to complete a software project.
Traditionally, the proposal might involve a team of developers, testers and project managers working over several months.
The price would reflect the people and time required.
Now imagine that AI tools allow the same team to complete parts of the project much faster.
That's good news for the customer.
But it creates an awkward question for the service provider.
Should the customer pay less because fewer working hours are needed?
Or should the provider earn more because it delivers the same result with greater efficiency?
This tension sits behind some of the concerns surrounding traditional IT services companies.
Several major Indian technology brands have experienced sharp declines in estimated brand value, with AI disruption affecting expectations for their business models.
The challenge is particularly significant for companies accustomed to measuring projects through staffing and utilization.
AI increases the importance of discussing outcomes.
A client commissioning a system doesn't necessarily care how many hours were spent writing the code.
They care whether it works reliably, solves the intended problem and remains maintainable.
Of course, outcome-based contracts introduce risks.
A service provider needs to estimate complexity carefully and agree on what successful delivery actually means.
Unexpected requirements can make a fixed commitment expensive.
Still, the direction of the market seems clear.
As technology makes work faster, pricing models built mainly around the quantity of labor will face increasing scrutiny.

Yesterday I wrote that India is being bought as a hedge against the AI trade, and that the capital is concentrating. Part 1 ended with a promise: the real value is going somewhere most boards are not looking.

Here is the payoff. Three places, all visible this week.

1️⃣ The application layer, not the model layer.

Of the $114 million that went into Indian AI startups this week, the biggest cheque was $53 million to Dreamteam, an application-layer B2B company. Physical AI startup Humyn Labs raised $47 million — $26 million in equity led by Accel plus $21 million in venture debt. Disseqt AI raised $8 million for AI governance. The market is paying for deployment, data and control, not for another model.

2️⃣ Sovereign capability has become a procurement argument.

At Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, Sarvam AI's Vivek Raghavan made the case for Sarvam-105B — a 105-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model trained from scratch in India on IndiaAI Mission compute, built for 22 Indian languages and voice-first use. The question it forces on every CTO is blunt: do we own our AI, or do we keep renting it?

3️⃣ Talent is the real bottleneck, and the numbers are uncomfortable.

90% of Indian employers are expanding tech teams, yet 63% expect net reductions in tech headcount within 12-24 months, and 44% are hiring fewer entry-level developers than two years ago. AI-qualified developers command more than twice entry-level pay. 72% of employers say running AI tools costs as much as, or more than, junior talent for comparable work. Contract staffing in Indian IT grew 10.1% in FY26, against 2.3% for permanent roles.

4️⃣ And the exit problem nobody wants to name.

India has over 4,500 deep-tech startups and funding is flowing, yet the exit landscape stays thin. The bottleneck is not innovation. It is that too few Indian companies are buyers of deep tech.

✅ Do fund the unglamorous middle — data, integration, governance, change management.

✅ Do move a slice of your AI budget into reskilling the team you already have. It is cheaper than the market rate.

❌ Don't buy an AI narrative you cannot operate.

❌ Don't wait for a clearer picture. The picture is being drawn by whoever deploys first.

The leadership test of this decade is not who has the best model. It is who converts a $1.8 trillion global buildout into Indian productivity, Indian jobs and Indian margins — and who stays content renting someone else's.

Capital is rotating. Capability is not. Build the second one.

How to Read Tree Lab #1 (Labor Market Shock)
Core Question
Where can an individual create the greatest long-term value, stability, and fulfillment within the labor force—and endure sudden market disruptions?
1. Internal Foundation (Individual → Capabilities)
Individual: The person at the center of the career structure, shaped by real-world context, constraints, and objectives.
Attributes: Natural aptitudes, interests, temperament, and core traits that shape how a person learns and works.
Skills: Practical, current abilities a person can execute today.
Knowledge: Formal education, technical concepts, domain familiarity, and structured training.
Capabilities: The combined operational power of attributes, skills, and knowledge applied to real work.
2. Market Interface & Execution (Opportunities → Value Creation)
Labor Force Structures & Opportunities: The actual roles, industries, compensation models, and market openings where capabilities can plug in.
Career Pathways: Coherent multi-step trajectories (such as moving from foundational tech or problem-solving into cybersecurity, cloud, software, or AI systems) rather than isolated job hops.
Employment: Active placement within a role, business, contract, or enterprise structure.
Performance: How reliably and effectively the individual delivers outcomes inside that structure.
Advancement: Progression in responsibility, leverage, authority, or compensation over time.
Value Creation: Measurable economic, operational, or human value produced for employers, clients, or communities.
3. Disruption & Shock Mechanics (Labor Market Shock → Shock Zones)
Labor Market Shock: A sudden or structural external disruption—such as layoffs, automation/AI shifts, industry contraction, regulatory changes, or economic downturns—that interrupts normal progression or forces re-routing back to Career Pathways.
Shock Zones: Specific areas of heightened vulnerability, buffer capacity, or recovery friction during or before a disruption:
Exposure: Roles, tasks, or sectors directly threatened by automation, budget cuts, or structural downsizing.
Runway: Financial reserves, time, support networks, and capacity that buy room to maneuver during transition.
Transferability: How readily existing skills, domain judgment, and experience carry over into another structure or role without starting from scratch.
Re-Entry Friction: Obstacles slowing or blocking recovery—such as hiring freezes, credential/licensing lag, changing tech requirements, experience/age bias, or geographic mismatch.
tch existing or near-term capabilities.

Growth Zones: High-leverage areas where modest, focused investment produces disproportionate career advancement.
5. Recursive Loop (New Opportunities → Cycle Repeats)

The interview is a customer who only answers what you ask.

That's how one hiring index describes the test for forward deployed engineers, the title so many AI companies are hiring for right now.

The idea came from Palantir: put engineers inside the customer's company and build what they actually need. AI made it urgent, because a signed AI contract and a working AI deployment turn out to be very different things.

The headline number is huge. Indeed data shared with Business Insider in May showed FDE postings up roughly 729% year over year, with pay from about $170k to over $200k.

The November picture is calmer. The A10X FDE Index counted 723 openings at 115 companies:

• Demand has been flat since late October
• Only 6% of the roles are fully remote
• 1 in 4 never says "forward deployed" in the title (Applied AI Engineer, Customer Engineer, Solutions Engineer)
• Salesforce, Databricks, Palantir, OpenAI and AWS have the most open roles
As a developer in Lahore, that 6% is the line I read twice. This job is built around being in the room, so for most of us the useful part is the skill set behind it.

And those skills are exactly the ones AI agents haven't sped up. Pulling real requirements out of someone who can't quite say them. Scoping. Staying with a deployment until people actually use it.

You don't need the title to practice any of that. Join the next stakeholder call you can. Write the spec before the code. Stay with your feature after it ships.

The engineers who can do that will have options, on site or not.

WHY TRADITIONAL CAREER "PLAYBOOKS" ARE OBSOLETE IN THE AGE OF AI

Entry-level corporate jobs are disappearing and the traditional career ladder is changing with them.

For decades, the standard formula for career success was straightforward: earn a degree, land an entry-level role, and spend your first few years doing routine work debugging basic code, reviewing standard contracts, or drafting routine copy. That repetitive work wasn't just busywork; it was the apprenticeship that built the judgment needed for senior roles.
Today, AI executes those foundational "playbook" tasks in seconds. As Palantir CEO Alex Karp recently pointed out, if your education only trained you to follow established frameworks, you are competing directly with software.

So, who actually holds long-term career leverage in the age of AI? According to Karp, it comes down to two distinct groups whose work cannot be reduced to a set of instructions:

1. SKILLED TRADESPEOPLE: ELECTRICIANS, PLUMBERS, CARPENTERS, and WELDERS operate in unpredictable physical environments. While AI excels at abstract logic, physical perception and on-site judgment remain extraordinarily difficult to automate. When a pipe bursts in an old building with no blueprints, software can't fix it experienced human hands and senses do.

2. NEURODIVERGENT THINKERS: Individuals with dyslexia, ADHD, or autism often struggle with rigid, linear "playbooks." Instead, they learn to see problems holistically, connect unexpected dots, and spot anomalies that standard processes smooth over. What traditional hiring once viewed as friction is rapidly becoming a core competitive advantage.

Palantir is already acting on this shift launching fellowships that bypass college degrees entirely and actively recruiting neurodivergent builders for their unique problem-solving strengths.

As AI handles the routine execution, human value shifts toward physical mastery and unconventional thinking.
How is AI changing entry-level hiring and skill development in your industry?

#FutureOfWork #AI #CareerDevelopment #HiringTrends #Leadership

​A clean verification check only proves that an AI followed its instructions. It does not prove those instructions were right.

​That distinction is happening right now with the proposed AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. Independent checks confirmed that the 17 million lines of code written in Lean, a verification language that checks logical steps, compile without internal errors. Yet the mathematics community has not declared the problem solved.

​Mathematicians are now doing a different kind of audit. They are checking the premises.
​Specifically, they are inspecting the starting rules and formal definitions entered into Lean at the beginning. If a definition quietly alters the original math problem, or if a hidden assumption slipped into the setup, the compiler can still return a valid result for the wrong question.

​You face this exact exposure when you deploy AI systems and automated compliance checks inside your business.

​An AI model can follow your prompt with high accuracy. An automated policy engine can pass 100% of its tests. Both systems still create legal and financial liability if the starting assumptions are flawed.

​Consider what happens when a flawed premise goes unchecked:

​- Your team builds an automated privacy filter using an outdated definition of personal data, and sensitive customer records leak into a third-party model.

​- Your hiring tool passes every internal fairness test because the test measures an indirect trait instead of actual job performance.

- ​Your contract review agent flags standard clauses accurately, but it misses a new statutory requirement that nobody added to its rule set.

​To protect your organization as AI workflows scale, audit your starting inputs before you audit the final outputs. Verify your starting definitions, legal classifications, and risk thresholds before you automate enforcement. Review those premises whenever laws or business operations change.

​If you audit only the final output, you miss errors built into the system from the start.

​If your team needs an independent review of the legal and technical premises behind your AI workflows, message VitrifAI.
